note: Honest, sourced catalog. kind=action (FrameForge applies+reverts it), verify (read-only health check, never an 'action'), advise (BIOS/manual/in-game — we guide, we don't fake it). Every action records prior state before changing so revert is exact.
tokenNote: Advisory copy is TEMPLATED, never baked to one machine. {tokens} in summary/details/name are substituted from the live sysinfo result at render time (e.g. {ram.ratedMTs} <- sys.ram.ratedMTs, {storage.fastDiskName}, {gpu.vramGB}, {cpu.name}). If ANY token in a string resolves to null/0/empty, the UI must suppress that whole advisory rather than print a placeholder or a guess — the catalog must describe the user's machine, not the developer's.
showIfNote: showIf is an AND-list of conditions against the sysinfo result: { path, equals | notEquals | gt | exists }. A condition whose path is missing or null evaluates UNKNOWN, and an advisory with an unknown condition is hidden — never shown on an assumption.
profileScopeNote: profileScope says WHOSE settings a tweak changes: 'user' means it writes HKCU — the Windows profile of whichever account FrameForge is running as — and 'machine' means it does not. This field is documentation (doctrine rule 5: the catalog says exactly what will run); engine.ps1 does NOT trust it, it derives the same answer structurally by walking the op tree for an HKCU root. It matters because 'Run as administrator' can relaunch FrameForge under a DIFFERENT account: HKCU is then the helper's hive, so engine.ps1 refuses every profileScope='user' apply, revert and detect it cannot prove belongs to the person at the keyboard. Per-user tweaks never need administrator rights, so the fix is always to run FrameForge unelevated.
scopeNote: powercfg ops carry an explicit AC/DC scope. scope='ac' (the default) touches mains behaviour only and leaves battery behaviour alone; 'ac+dc' touches both and MUST say so in details. Detect reads exactly the indexes in scope, so the verify-after probe is never narrower than the apply.

tweaks.name: Disable Game DVR background recording
tweaks.summary: Turns off the Xbox Game Bar background recorder.
tweaks.details: Game DVR continuously buffers gameplay so you can 'record that'. That capture costs GPU encoder time and CPU and is one of the most reliably measurable FPS/stutter wins when turned off.
tweaks.evidence: Reproduced in many before/after captures; the background DVR thread competes for the GPU encoder.

tweaks.name: Windows Game Mode
tweaks.summary: Ensures Game Mode is on so Windows defers background work while you play.
tweaks.details: Game Mode suppresses background interruptions (driver installs, defrag, Update installs) during a game, reducing stutter from background CPU spikes. Low but free.
tweaks.evidence: Microsoft-documented behavior prioritizing the active game.

tweaks.name: Performance power plan (no min-state pin)
tweaks.summary: Activates the Ultimate Performance plan (High Performance on battery-powered systems) and explicitly UN-pins minimum processor state.
tweaks.details: Removes CPU core parking and idle-demotion latency for steadier frametimes. Crucially, FrameForge sets minimum processor state to 5% (NOT 100%) — on a 13th/14th-gen Intel chip, pinning min state at 100% keeps cores out of low-power states and raises the idle voltage floor, the exact condition linked to Raptor Lake Vmin-shift aging. This gives the latency benefit without the aging risk. WHAT ACTUALLY RUNS: Windows does not offer the Ultimate Performance plan on battery-powered systems, so on a laptop, 2-in-1, tablet or handheld FrameForge activates the built-in High Performance plan (8c5e7fda-…) instead and says so. The minimum-processor-state change is written to BOTH the mains (AC) and battery (DC) indexes of the plan it activates — on a laptop that changes battery behaviour too — and the plan's prior values are captured first so undo restores them exactly. Undo switches back to the plan that was active before; a duplicated plan is left in Power Options (inactive, harmless) rather than deleted.
tweaks.evidence: Intel guidance against sustained elevated voltage on Raptor Lake; power-plan core-parking removal reduces scheduling latency.

tweaks.name: Disable Windows Update P2P (Delivery Optimization)
tweaks.summary: Stops Windows from uploading/downloading updates peer-to-peer in the background.
tweaks.details: Delivery Optimization can use your bandwidth and CPU to seed Windows/Store updates to other PCs while you game, causing latency spikes and bandwidth contention. Setting download mode to HTTP-only (no peering) keeps updates working but ends the background P2P. WHAT ACTUALLY RUNS: this is the one FrameForge action that writes into the Group Policy hive (HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\…\DeliveryOptimization\DODownloadMode), because that is the only documented location for DODownloadMode. On a domain-joined or MDM/Intune-managed machine the policy engine rewrites that key at its next refresh, so FrameForge REFUSES the tweak there instead of reporting an 'Applied' that quietly expires — ask your administrator to set Delivery Optimization download mode instead.
tweaks.evidence: Documented DODownloadMode policy; mode 0 disables peering.

tweaks.name: Trim desktop animations (cosmetic)
tweaks.summary: Disables window/taskbar animations for a snappier desktop and overlays.
tweaks.details: Cosmetic: negligible effect on fullscreen in-game FPS, but reduces compositor work so Alt-Tab and overlays feel instant. Tagged honestly as low/cosmetic.
tweaks.evidence: DWM animation cost; perceptual snappiness, not FPS.

tweaks.name: Disable mouse acceleration (Enhance Pointer Precision)
tweaks.summary: Turns off Windows pointer acceleration for 1:1, consistent aim.
tweaks.details: Enhance Pointer Precision speeds the cursor up the faster you move, so the same physical motion maps to different in-game angles. Competitive players disable it for muscle-memory consistency. This affects aim consistency / input feel, not FPS. Fully reversible.
tweaks.evidence: Raw, acceleration-free input is the standard competitive configuration; 1:1 mapping is reproducible.

tweaks.name: Disable USB selective suspend (on mains power)
tweaks.summary: Stops Windows from power-gating USB devices (mouse/keyboard/controller) while you are on mains power.
tweaks.details: USB selective suspend lets Windows put idle USB devices to sleep to save power. On a gaming desktop this can cause brief input-device hitches or micro-disconnects. Disabling it keeps your peripherals always-on. WHAT ACTUALLY RUNS: FrameForge writes the AC (plugged-in) index ONLY, in the active power plan. Battery (DC) behaviour is deliberately left alone, because keeping USB endpoints awake on battery measurably shortens runtime — so on a laptop this tweak applies on mains power and nowhere else, and detect reports it that way. Reversible: FrameForge records the prior AC value and restores exactly that, and refuses to claim a successful undo if the prior value could not be read.
tweaks.evidence: Selective suspend power-gates idle USB endpoints; disabling removes wake latency for input devices.

tweaks.name: Hardware-Accelerated GPU Scheduling
tweaks.summary: Should be ON — required for NVIDIA Reflex and DLSS Frame Generation latency paths.
tweaks.details: HAGS lets the GPU manage its own frame queue, reducing CPU overhead and enabling the lowest-latency Reflex/Frame-Gen paths on RTX 40/50-series. We verify it's on rather than toggling it (toggling needs a reboot). If the HwSchMode value is absent — no WDDM 2.7+ GPU, or a driver that never wrote it — FrameForge reports 'could not determine' rather than 'off'.
tweaks.evidence: NVIDIA requires HAGS for the Reflex/Frame-Generation low-latency pipeline.

tweaks.name: Raptor Lake microcode (Vmin-shift mitigation)
tweaks.summary: Confirms a desktop Intel 13th/14th-gen CPU is on the patched microcode that mitigates the Vmin-shift instability.
tweaks.details: Intel's 0x12B microcode (and BIOS updates) address the Vmin-shift degradation that affected some 13th/14th-gen K chips. This is a stability/longevity check, not an FPS toggle — but a degrading chip silently loses performance and crashes. If your microcode is older, update the BIOS. SCOPE: microcode revision numbers are per-CPUID, so this check only runs on a DESKTOP Intel Raptor Lake S part (CPUID family 6, model 0xB7/0xBF, non-battery form factor). On any other CPU — AMD, ARM64, Intel 12th-gen and older, Core Ultra, or a mobile 13th/14th-gen part — the check is hidden and excluded from the score instead of being answered from a number that means something else.

tweaks.name: Receive Side Scaling (NIC)
tweaks.summary: Should be ON so network interrupts spread across CPU cores.
tweaks.details: RSS distributes NIC interrupt processing across multiple cores instead of pinning core 0. Default-on; we verify it rather than 'fixing' something that isn't broken. If no adapter could actually be queried — an unelevated session where Get-NetAdapterRss is refused, only virtual/USB adapters, or no NIC up — FrameForge reports 'could not determine' and the check is excluded from the score, instead of showing a green tick for a measurement that never happened.
tweaks.evidence: Documented RSS behavior; default-enabled on modern adapters.

tweaks.name: Intel Default Settings power profile (BIOS — do FIRST)
tweaks.summary: Apply the Intel-recommended power guardrail (PL1/PL2/ICCMax) in BIOS before any memory OC.
tweaks.details: Many boards ship with an 'unlimited' power default that can push a 13th/14th-gen part past Intel's spec, contributing to instability and aging. Set the Intel Default Settings (Performance profile: PL1/PL2 = 253W, ICCMax = 307A on K-series desktop parts) in BIOS first. This protects the chip and is the recommended ordering BEFORE enabling XMP.
tweaks.evidence: Intel Default Settings guidance for Raptor Lake stability (2024).
guide: Reboot and press your board's setup key at the splash screen (usually Del, sometimes F2)
Find the CPU power/cooler tuning section (often labelled 'Intel Default Settings' or 'CPU Cooler Tuning')
Choose 'Intel Default Settings' -> 'Performance'
Save & Exit (usually F10)

tweaks.name: Enable XMP/EXPO memory profile (BIOS — do AFTER Intel Default Settings)
tweaks.summary: Your RAM runs {ram.runningMTs} MT/s but is rated {ram.ratedMTs} MT/s — enabling XMP/EXPO is the single biggest free CPU-bound FPS lever available here.
tweaks.details: Memory bandwidth and latency are among the largest CPU-bound FPS levers on a modern desktop. FrameForge measured your modules running at {ram.runningMTs} MT/s against a rated {ram.ratedMTs} MT/s, which means the memory profile is off. Enabling XMP (Intel) or EXPO (AMD) Profile 1 typically yields high-single-digit to mid-teens % gains in CPU-bound titles. On an Intel platform do this AFTER setting Intel Default Settings so the platform is stable first. BIOS-only — Windows cannot toggle it. This advisory is hidden entirely when the running or rated speed could not be read, or when they already match: it describes your modules, not anyone else's.
tweaks.evidence: Outlet 1080p CPU-bound benchmarks: JEDEC base speed vs the rated XMP/EXPO profile delivers large avg and 1%-low uplifts on recent desktop platforms.
guide: Reboot and press your board's setup key at the splash screen (usually Del, sometimes F2)
Find the XMP / EXPO switch (often on the first screen) or the Extreme Memory Profile entry under the OC/Tweaker menu
Select Profile 1 ({ram.ratedMTs} MT/s)
Save & Exit. If it fails to POST, clear CMOS and try the board's manual memory tuning at the rated speed.

tweaks.name: Resizable BAR (BIOS)
tweaks.summary: Let the CPU address all of your card's VRAM at once instead of a 256MB window — verify it's enabled.
tweaks.details: Resizable BAR removes the 256MB VRAM aperture limit and can improve performance in some titles. On a modern discrete GPU + UEFI platform it should be on. Verify it in your GPU vendor's control panel (NVIDIA App -> System -> Resizable BAR; AMD Software -> Performance) or in BIOS (Re-Size BAR Support = Enabled, which requires Above 4G Decoding). Gains are title-dependent and can be negative in a few games — this is a 'check it is on', not a promise.
guide: Open your GPU vendor's control panel and look for 'Resizable BAR'
If Off: reboot -> BIOS -> PCIe/Advanced -> enable 'Above 4G Decoding' and 'Re-Size BAR Support'
Save & Exit

tweaks.name: Enable NVIDIA Reflex in-game
tweaks.summary: The real latency win — turn Reflex On/On+Boost in each game that supports it.
tweaks.details: NVIDIA Reflex reduces render-queue latency far more effectively than any driver/registry tweak, often 20–40ms. Prefer the in-game Reflex toggle over the driver's Low Latency Mode. Pair with HAGS on and a frame cap below your refresh.
tweaks.evidence: NVIDIA Reflex measured click-to-photon latency reductions across supported titles.
guide: In each supported game's Video/Graphics settings, find 'NVIDIA Reflex Low Latency'
Set it to 'On' (or 'On + Boost' for the lowest latency)
Keep HAGS enabled and cap FPS just below your refresh for the best latency

tweaks.name: Prefer a wired connection
tweaks.summary: For online games, a wired connection slashes latency variance versus Wi-Fi.
tweaks.details: Wi-Fi adds jitter and packet loss that no registry tweak can fix. FrameForge sees you routing over {network.activeAdapter} and sees a wired adapter available on this machine, so plugging in is worth it for competitive play. This affects ping and consistency, not raw FPS. Hidden when you are already wired, or when this machine has no wired adapter at all — a thin laptop with no Ethernet port should never be told to plug one in.
tweaks.evidence: Wired vs Wi-Fi latency-jitter is well established.
guide: Plug an Ethernet cable into your machine's Ethernet port (or a USB/Thunderbolt adapter)
Windows will prefer the wired route automatically when it is connected

tweaks.name: Move active games to your fastest drive
tweaks.summary: {storage.slowGameCount} installed game(s) sit on slower storage while {storage.fastDiskName} is available.
tweaks.details: A SATA SSD (and far more so a mechanical drive) is slower than NVMe for texture streaming and shader compilation, which shows up as traversal stutter and longer shader-comp hitches. Keep the library you actually play, and the shader cache, on {storage.fastDiskName}. This advisory only appears when FrameForge has positively identified BOTH a slower drive holding games and a faster drive to move them to — a single-drive machine, or one whose disks could not be classified, never sees it.
tweaks.evidence: SATA/QLC sustained-write and random-read deficits versus NVMe TLC affect streaming and shader-compilation stutter.
guide: In Steam: Settings -> Storage -> add or select {storage.fastDiskName} -> move your active games there
Keep the OS (and therefore the driver shader cache) on the fastest drive as well

tweaks.name: Disable Nagle's algorithm (TCP games only)
tweaks.summary: Advise-only: helps a few TCP-based games, useless for UDP shooters (CS2/Valorant/Apex).
tweaks.details: Nagle batches small TCP packets, adding a few ms. Disabling can help latency in TCP-based online games, but most competitive shooters use UDP where this does nothing. Because it requires fragile per-interface GUID matching and a reboot, FrameForge advises rather than auto-applies it.
tweaks.evidence: Nagle batching delay applies only to TCP; UDP titles unaffected.
guide: Only do this for TCP-based games
Under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\Tcpip\Parameters\Interfaces\{your-active-GUID}, add DWORD TcpAckFrequency=1 and TCPNoDelay=1
Reboot. Remove both values to revert.
